extracted.intended_audience: NIH principal investigators, grant applicants, and research administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Practical discussion and informal guidance about no-cost extensions (NCEs) on NIH grants: what they mean administratively, how reviewers may perceive them, how to report them in biosketches/progress reports, and financial/carryover rules to watch for.

rubrics_metrics.name: No-cost extension (NCE) definition and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: When the interval of support ends the PI (actually the University or Institute) can request a NCE so the NIH will not give additional money but the University may continue to spend any un-expended funds. NCE requests, particularly the first year, are often approved by default.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request an NCE when a competing renewal hasn't been approved in time; many experienced PIs request NCEs 'by default' for awards that permit them. Be aware of local institutional red tape reasons for doing so and check how NCEs interact with your renewal submission practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carryover limit (25% rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Usual rules for rolling money apply — it is supposed to be only 25% of the prior year or less that can be carried forward. The 25% carryover limit has long been in place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm with your institution and grants office. There is discussion whether the first year of an NCE is exempt from the 25% calculation; if NCE extends beyond one year NIH approval is required and the 25% rule definitely applies. Check award-specific terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: NCE effect on renewals/competing continuation eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A renewal (competing continuation) application does not require that the original grant still be active — there is no time limit for submitting a renewal — but reviewers will probably be concerned by major gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a significant amount of time has elapsed, explicitly indicate what you did in the interim, highlight any preliminary data obtained, and show that the planned research is current with the latest science to mitigate reviewer concern about gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listing NCE in biosketch/research support (ongoing vs completed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate exists about whether an NCE 'counts' as current research funding. Many biosketches list grants in NCE as 'ongoing' but marked as no-cost-extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List NCE grants under 'ongoing' Research Support and mark them as no-cost-extension to be transparent; be prepared that perceptions vary among reviewers about whether NCE counts as active funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer perspective: focus on future plan and track record
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers tend to care less about 'working on the project' during the prior interval and more about the applicant's plan for the future and evidence of productivity/track record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize a strong plan for the proposed work and past progress/productivity rather than relying on the fact that a project was in NCE to convey ongoing activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception risk of multiple NCEs
rubrics_metrics.description: Listing more than one grant in NCE (or many NCEs) can look bad to some readers/reviewers, whereas a single NCE is common and often not noteworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid giving the impression of repeatedly postponing completion; if multiple NCEs exist, explain circumstances and justify progress and plans for completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on additional funding during NCE
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency cannot provide yearly supplements during the NCE period — you cannot receive additional funds for that project while it is in NCE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need additional funds during that time inquire with your Program Manager whether renewals are treated as new awards (which could affect supplement eligibility) and plan budgets accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Award- and institution-specific terms may vary
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard NIH terms may not include a 25% limit for automatic NCE, but a specific award or awarding IC can impose more restrictive terms; some institutions treat the first year of NCE as internal authorization only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always check the specific terms of your award and your university's grants management policies rather than assuming a single universal rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting unobligated balance in progress reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress report instructions: 'Is it anticipated that an estimated unobligated balance (including prior year carryover) will be greater than 25% of the current year’s total approved budget?' The 'total approved budget' equals the current fiscal year award authorization plus any approved carryover; the numerator equals total amount available for carryover and the denominator equals the current year’s total approved budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand how NIH counts carryover and unobligated balances when preparing progress reports; practices or interpretation changes can affect whether multiple years of savings accumulate, so consult institutional experts if unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic use of NCE to buy time (spending planning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experienced PIs, especially on soft money, use NCEs to buy time and plan spending so grants last longer than originally budgeted (e.g., aiming for resources to last an extra year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conservatively plan expenditures and consider retaining funds to cover a potential NCE period. However, follow carryover rules and institutional approvals and avoid accumulating amounts that would violate the 25% guidance or award terms.
